optionReasons.saa-avc-002:option:1: Security Group network control — does not filter items by partition key within a table DynamoDB.
optionReasons.saa-avc-002:option:2: It's the closest because a table per user ALSO would isolate the data — but not scale for multi-tenant (thousands of tables, account limits, unfeasible cost and operation) and it's not 'restriction on credentials'; the request is to restrict by partition key in the credentials itself, which the LeadingKeys condition delivers.
optionReasons.saa-avc-002:option:3: Full access to all authenticated is the opposite of isolation per user requested.

finalJustifications: Because the condition dynamodb:LeadingKeys links the federated credentials to the user's partition key — each only reads and writes its own items in the same table.
Because the LeadingKeys condition creates a logic table isolated by user within physics, partitioning access without multiplying resources.
Because the LeadingKeys condition applies a Security Group by partition key, filtering into the network layer the items that each user reaches.
Because the LeadingKeys condition grants full access to DynamoDB and then filter the customer response according to the user ID.

optionReasons.saa-avc-003:option:0: Elastic IP in EC2 exposes the API on the internet and still throws out all the management of API Gateway.
optionReasons.saa-avc-003:option:2: It is the closest because the Regional is indeed a kind of endpoint of API Gateway — but it is PUBLIC on the Internet: even restricted by politics, resolves by DNS public and does not attend 'accessible only from within the VPC'; the Private type via VPC Endpoint (PrivateLink) maintains internal traffic.
optionReasons.saa-avc-003:option:3: Edge-Optimized distributes over the global edge of CloudFront — the most public of all types.

finalJustifications: Because API Gateway Private is only reachable by VPC Interface Endpoint (PrivateLink): traffic is within the VPC and never touches the public internet.
Because API Gateway Private routes along the edge of the CloudFront with private IP, delivering low latency without publicly exposing the endpoint.
Because API Gateway Private combines an internal Elastic IP with VPC, and the bodies call the API by this fixed and reserved address.
Because API Gateway Private applies a resource policy that blocks the internet at the Regional Endpoint, making it private by configuration.

optionReasons.saa-avc-005:option:0: Change for DynamoDB 'without changing the rest' would rewrite the data model — it is not resilience adjustment of the Aurora.
optionReasons.saa-avc-005:option:1: Monthly backup for the S3 Yes RPO up to one month — the opposite end of 'near zero'.
optionReasons.saa-avc-005:option:2: It's the closest because it's still Aurora and quotes snapshots — but a single instance in UMA AZ with daily snapshot gives RPO up to 24h and no protection against regional failure; RPO close to zero and RTO low between regions only Aurora Global Database delivery, with low latency replication.

finalJustifications: Because Aurora Global Database replicates for a subsecond-late region — RPO near zero and rapid promotion of the replica in regional failure.
Because Aurora Global Database keeps daily snapshots in the secondary region, restored in minutes when the primary region falls whole.
Because Aurora Global Database converts the table to the global model DynamoDB, inheriting multi-region replication without touching the application.
Because Aurora Global Database exports transaction log to the S3 continuously, and the secondary region reimports it in case of disaster.

optionReasons.saa-avc-006:option:0: The Lambda does not process 'always exactly 3 times' — invented number; redelivery depends on row and timeout, not fixed.
optionReasons.saa-avc-006:option:2: It's the closest because it actually points to the consumer — but part of a premise FALSA: o SQS Standard DOES NOT guarantee exactly-once; it delivers 'at least once' by design, then fix only the code without idempotence (or without FIFO) does not eliminate duplicates.
optionReasons.saa-avc-006:option:3: The problem is solveable with SQS (Idempotence or FIFO) — migrate to the Kinesis is unnecessary.

finalJustifications: Because SQS Standard is at-last-once by design: mitigation is to make the consumer idempotent — or use FIFO with deduplication when order and uniqueness matter.
Because SQS Standard is exactly-once, so just fix the consumer bug that reprocesses the message, without any change in the queue itself.
Because Lambda deliver each message three times per default, and reduce this number in function settings eliminates duplicate effects.
Because SQS can't guarantee uniqueness in any way, and the only way out is to migrate the entire pipeline to the Kinesis Data Streams.

optionReasons.saa-avc-007:option:1: Field-Level Encryption protects sensitive fields from payload — nothing to do with availability of origin.
optionReasons.saa-avc-007:option:2: It's the closest because the Lambda@Edge REALMENTE spins on the edge and can handle requests — but 'just for cache' does not redirect to a secondary origin during the fall of the primary; automatic failure between origins is Origin Failover with Origin Groups.
optionReasons.saa-avc-007:option:3: Signed URLs control who accesses the content — do not treat source failure.

finalJustifications: Because Origin Group defines primary and secondary origin: when detecting failure or error status in primary, the CloudFront automatically serves by the secondary.
Because Origin Failover performs a function Lambda@Edge rewrites the cache pointing to the secondary region during maintenance.
Because Origin Failover encrypts sensitive fields before changing origin, ensuring the safe continuity of service.
Because Origin Failover signs the URLs of secondary origin, and only authorized requests are diverted when the primary falls.

optionReasons.saa-avc-008:option:0: It's the closest because the EBS gp2 is also low latency storage — but is BLOCO attached to UMA instance: not shared among hundreds of EC2 nor does it deliver the aggregate throughput of HPC; shared parallel file system is the FSx for Lustre.
optionReasons.saa-avc-008:option:1: Tape Gateway is virtual tape library for backup — nothing to do with throughput from HPC shared.
optionReasons.saa-avc-008:option:3: Glacier Deep Archive is cold filing with recovery in hours — the opposite of low latency.

finalJustifications: Because FSx for Lustre is the parallel file system of HPC: High throughput and low latency shared among hundreds of instances EC2 at the same time.
Because the FSx for Lustre attachs a high performance gp2 volume to each instance, and the sum of the volumes delivers the throughput of the load of HPC.
Because FSx for Lustre exposes the Tape Gateway virtual tapes as a file system, read in parallel by video processing instances.
Because FSx for Lustre serves the data directly from the Glacier Deep Archive, and the local cache compensates for archival recovery latency.

optionReasons.saa-avc-009:option:1: It's the closest because the Geographic also routes by location and seems 'less latency' — but it decides by the location of the user, not by latency REAL measure to the Region, and SEM health checks does not fail: the fallen region would continue receiving traffic; less latency with failover is Latency-based + health checks.
optionReasons.saa-avc-009:option:2: Simple Routing returns a fixed record — no notion of latenity or endpoint health.
optionReasons.saa-avc-009:option:3: Weighted 100% in a single region sends everything to a place — does not optimize latency or tolerate failure.

finalJustifications: Because Latency-based Routing sends each user to the region with the lowest latency measured, and health checks remove the region from the available route automatically.
Because latency router decides on the geographical location of the user and reevaluates the health of the Region only in the next consultation of DNS.
Because simple routing returns the lowest latency endpoint and alternates to another region as soon as the health check accuses failure in the current.
Because the weighted router divides the latency traffic of each region, adjusting the weights alone as the health checks respond.

optionReasons.saa-avc-010:option:0: DynamoDB Streams captures changes — disable it has no connection to hot partition.
optionReasons.saa-avc-010:option:1: It's the closest because the most RCU/WCU looks like the obvious exit to throttling — but the gargalo is DISTRIBUTION: a hot partition has its own limit (~1.000 WCU/3.000 RCU) and some capacity does not pass from that ceiling by partition; the problem only goes by redistributing the key (write sharding)).
optionReasons.saa-avc-010:option:3: Migrate everything to the S3 swaps the access bank by key for storage of objects — is not key redesign.

finalJustifications: Because write sharding spreads items through various partitions (random/calculated suffix on the key), eliminating the hot partition that causes localized throttling.
Because increasing the provided capacity raises the ceiling per roofless partition, and the throttling disappears as soon as the RCU/WCU ♪ they're up high enough ♪.
Why disable the DynamoDB Streams releases the capacity that the capture of changes consumed, easing the pressure on the hot partition.
Why migrate the table to the S3 distributes the items by object prefixes, and the partitioning of the bucket resolves the concentrated key.
